_meta.description: Reference ranges for liver panel + PBC-specific markers, in SI units as commonly reported on Kazakhstani/Russian lab printouts (not US conventional units). Adult ranges; not age/sex-exhaustive for a v1.
_meta.disclaimer: For patient education only. Not a diagnostic tool. All critical thresholds must trigger escalation to a physician, never an independent conclusion.
_meta.kz_translations_note: Kazakh medical terms provided as a first pass; review with a native-speaking clinician before production use.
sources: AASLD Practice Guidance: Primary Biliary Cholangitis 2018 update
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: The diagnosis and management of patients with primary biliary cholangitis 2017
AASLD/EASL cirrhosis and complications guidance (ascites, hepatic encephalopathy)
Standard clinical chemistry reference intervals (adult, SI units) -- most normal_low/normal_high values here, since routine lab reference intervals are physiological, not protocol-specific

Kazakhstan MoH Clinical Protocol for Liver Cirrhosis, 2020 (Protocol No. 135, see rag/corpus/clinical/02_kz_protocol_cirrhosis.md) -- specifically informs the CREATININE critical_high note (HRS Type I criteria) and is the source for the FibroScan F4 cutoff referenced in cirrhosis_note text; the protocol does not publish its own separate numeric reference ranges for routine markers, which is why most other fields cite general clinical chemistry standards instead

markers.cirrhosis_note: In cirrhosis, ALT can be normal or only mildly elevated even with active disease — a normal ALT does not rule out progression. Trend matters more than a single value.
An AST/ALT ratio > 1 is common in cirrhosis regardless of underlying cause.
markers.udca_response_role: Paris-II criterion: AST ≤ 1.5x ULN (≤60 U/L) after 1 year of UDCA therapy indicates adequate biochemical response.

markers.cirrhosis_note: Typically elevated in PBC as a cholestatic marker; tracked alongside ALP rather than in isolation.
The central cholestatic marker for PBC monitoring — sustained elevation reflects ongoing bile-duct injury.
markers.udca_response_role: Paris-II criterion: ALP ≤ 1.5x ULN (≤225 U/L) after 1 year of UDCA therapy indicates adequate biochemical response; failure to reach this threshold should prompt discussion of second-line therapy with the treating physician.

markers.cirrhosis_note: Rising bilirubin is one of the strongest single markers of worsening liver synthetic/excretory function and feeds directly into the MELD-Na score.
markers.udca_response_role: Paris-II criterion: bilirubin within the normal range after 1 year of UDCA therapy is required for an adequate biochemical response.

markers.cirrhosis_note: A rising direct fraction points specifically to cholestasis, consistent with PBC's mechanism.
Reflects the liver's synthetic function; a falling albumin over time (not one low reading) is the meaningful signal and also feeds Child-Pugh scoring.
Interpreted alongside albumin and globulin fraction; a wide albumin-globulin gap can reflect chronic liver disease.
Reflects synthetic (clotting-factor) function; a key input to both MELD-Na and Child-Pugh scores. Rising INR is a serious signal.

Mild-to-moderate thrombocytopenia (roughly 100-150) is EXPECTED in cirrhosis due to portal hypertension and splenic sequestration — this is not, by itself, alarming and should be explained calmly, not flagged as a new problem, unless it falls sharply or crosses the critical threshold.

Part of the routine CBC (ОАК) panel, added after real-usage feedback asked for CBC markers alongside biochemistry. Mild leukopenia can accompany hypersplenism in cirrhosis, same mechanism as the thrombocytopenia note above.
Part of the routine CBC (ОАК) panel. Tracked alongside hemoglobin/hematocrit for anemia, which can relate to GI bleeding risk from varices in advanced cirrhosis.
Part of the routine CBC (ОАК) panel. Low hemoglobin (anemia) is clinically relevant in cirrhosis -- can reflect chronic disease, nutritional issues, or GI bleeding from varices.
Part of the routine CBC (ОАК) panel, tracked alongside hemoglobin.

Renal function is tightly linked to liver disease severity (hepatorenal risk) and is a direct MELD-Na input. The KZ MoH protocol (02_kz_protocol_cirrhosis.md) defines Hepatorenal Syndrome Type I specifically as creatinine doubling to >220 umol/L within 2 weeks -- a dynamic (rate-of-change) criterion the app's trend logic should check in addition to this static critical_high threshold.
Low sodium is common with ascites/diuretic use; a sharp drop below the critical threshold is a recognized marker of decompensation and a direct MELD-Na input.

Used as part of routine HCC (liver cancer) surveillance in cirrhosis patients — a rising value, even within range, should always be routed to escalation for physician review rather than explained away.

The hallmark diagnostic antibody for PBC (positive in ~90-95% of patients). Some Kazakhstani/Russian labs report it quantitatively (IU/mL, e.g. a real observed value of 59 IU/mL against a ~<25 IU/mL negative cutoff) rather than purely qualitatively. Not a monitoring marker for disease activity — once positive, it is tracked for record-keeping/history, not trended for severity like ALP/bilirubin are.

Raw seconds form of the same clotting-time measurement INR is derived from; Kazakhstani coagulation panels typically report PT (sec), PTI (%), and INR together. Prefer the lab's own printed reference range on each report over this default, since reagent-dependent variation is common.
An alternative expression of clotting function alongside PT/INR, commonly reported on KZ/RU lab panels. A falling PTI alongside a rising INR reinforces the same synthetic-function signal.
Part of the routine coagulation panel; reflects a different part of the clotting cascade than PT/INR. Prolongation supports the same synthetic-dysfunction picture.
A clotting factor synthesized by the liver; low fibrinogen supports reduced synthetic function and adds bleeding risk alongside a low platelet count.
Completes the routine KZ/RU coagulation panel alongside PT/PTI/INR/aPTT/fibrinogen; interpreted as part of the same synthetic-function cluster, not in isolation.
Characteristically elevated in PBC; can be tracked as a supportive (not primary) activity marker alongside ALP/bilirubin.

Reflects kidney function more directly than liver function, but tracked here because advanced liver disease can affect both hepatorenal status and urea synthesis itself (the liver produces urea); a low value can reflect reduced synthetic function rather than a kidney problem, so interpret alongside creatinine and albumin.

Usually calculated as total minus direct bilirubin. In PBC/cholestasis the DIRECT fraction typically rises proportionally more -- a mostly-indirect rise instead points toward a different mechanism (e.g. increased red cell breakdown) and is worth flagging to the doctor rather than assumed to be liver-related.

ESR is a non-specific marker of inflammation and is not a liver-specific test — it can be elevated in infections, autoimmune conditions, anemia, and many other states. In PBC it may be mildly elevated due to the underlying autoimmune/inflammatory process, but it is not used to assess liver function or fibrosis/cirrhosis severity; it's typically tracked as a general inflammatory marker rather than for direct liver monitoring.

markers.marker_name_ru: Измерение скорости оседания эритроцитов (СОЭ) в крови на анализаторе
markers.marker_name_kz: Қандағы эритроциттердің тұну жылдамдығын (ЭТЖ) анализатормен өлшеу

markers.marker_name_ru: Среднее содержание гемоглобина в эритроците (MCH, цветной показатель)
markers.marker_name_kz: Эритроциттегі гемоглобиннің орташа мөлшері (MCH, түстік көрсеткіш)

markers.cirrhosis_note: Neutrophil percentage is a component of the white blood cell differential and is not a liver-specific marker; it's typically used to assess infection, inflammation, or bone marrow/immune status. In PBC/cirrhosis patients it can be mildly relevant indirectly (e.g., if infection or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is suspected, or if hypersplenism from portal hypertension is affecting blood counts), but it does not directly reflect liver function or fibrosis and should not be used to track cirrhosis progression itself.

Lymphocyte percentage is a general white blood cell differential component, not a liver-specific marker. In PBC/cirrhosis it's usually tracked as part of a routine complete blood count to screen for infection, hypersplenism-related cytopenias, or bone marrow effects, rather than to assess liver function or fibrosis directly.

Monocyte percentage is a general white blood cell differential component, not a liver-specific marker; it's typically used to assess infection, inflammation, or hematologic disorders. In PBC/cirrhosis patients it may be tracked incidentally as part of a routine CBC (e.g., if hypersplenism or infection is suspected), but it does not directly reflect liver function or fibrosis progression.

Eosinophils are part of the white blood cell differential and are NOT a liver-specific marker; they are typically tracked for allergic reactions, parasitic infections, and drug hypersensitivity. In PBC patients, mild eosinophilia is occasionally seen (e.g., early PBC or drug reactions like ursodeoxycholic acid intolerance), but this marker is not used to monitor liver fibrosis or cirrhosis progression directly.

Basophils are not a liver-specific marker; they are part of the white blood cell differential and mainly used to assess allergic reactions, certain inflammatory conditions, or rare myeloproliferative disorders. In PBC/cirrhosis patients this value is typically just monitored as part of routine CBC surveillance rather than as an indicator of liver disease severity or progression.

This is not a liver-specific marker; it's a component of the white blood cell differential used mainly to assess bacterial infection, inflammation, or bone marrow function. In cirrhosis/PBC patients it can be indirectly relevant because advanced cirrhosis with splenomegaly/hypersplenism may lower neutrophil counts, and infections (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) can raise them, but it does not measure liver damage or cholestasis directly.

Absolute lymphocyte count is a general hematology/immune marker (part of the CBC differential), not a liver-specific test. In PBC/cirrhosis it's mainly useful for detecting hypersplenism-related cytopenias (low counts with splenomegaly/portal hypertension) or infection/inflammatory states, rather than directly reflecting liver damage; it does not track disease activity like ALT, ALP, or bilirubin do.

Monocytes are part of the general white blood cell differential and are not a liver-specific marker; they are typically used to assess infection, inflammation, or hematologic conditions rather than to monitor PBC/cirrhosis progression directly. In PBC patients, mild elevations may occur alongside general inflammatory activity, but this value should not be used as a primary indicator of liver disease severity or cholestasis - markers like ALP, GGT, bilirubin, and albumin remain the key liver-specific parameters to track.

Eosinophil count is not a liver-specific marker — it's part of the white blood cell differential and is mainly used to track allergic reactions, drug hypersensitivity, parasitic infections, and some autoimmune conditions. In PBC patients it can occasionally rise as a reaction to medications (e.g., ursodeoxycholic acid or other drugs) or reflect a concurrent allergic/autoimmune process, but it does not directly indicate liver fibrosis, cholestasis, or disease progression.

Basophils are not a liver-specific marker; they are part of the routine complete blood count (CBC) and mainly reflect allergic/inflammatory or, rarely, myeloproliferative processes. In PBC/cirrhosis patients this value is usually just monitored as part of general blood count surveillance rather than for liver-specific disease activity, though marked changes could reflect concurrent inflammation, infection, or hypersplenism-related bone marrow/spleen effects seen in advanced liver disease.

markers.marker_name_en: Red Cell Distribution Width - Standard Deviation (RDW-SD)

markers.cirrhosis_note: MPV is not a liver-specific marker — it's a routine CBC platelet index used mainly to assess platelet production/turnover and cardiovascular or clotting risk. In PBC/cirrhosis patients it can shift secondarily as platelet counts fall due to portal hypertension/hypersplenism (larger, younger platelets released to compensate for low count), so it's worth noting alongside the platelet count trend, but it should not be interpreted as a direct measure of liver damage or fibrosis.

Glucose is not a liver-specific marker — it's primarily used to screen for and monitor diabetes/prediabetes and general metabolic status. That said, advanced liver cirrhosis (including PBC-related cirrhosis) can impair glucose regulation, sometimes causing hepatogenous diabetes (high glucose) or, less commonly, hypoglycemia in severe liver failure, so it's still reasonable to track alongside liver-specific tests.

Potassium is not a liver-specific marker; it's an electrolyte reflecting kidney function, acid-base balance, and diuretic effects. In PBC/cirrhosis patients it's still important to monitor because diuretics (e.g., spironolactone or furosemide used for ascites/edema) and complications like hepatorenal syndrome can cause dangerous hyper- or hypokalemia, so it's tracked as part of routine safety labs rather than as a direct measure of liver damage.

This is not a clinical lab marker at all — "Количество" (Quantity, in mL) simply records the volume of the biological specimen (e.g., urine or fluid) submitted for testing, a pre-analytical/collection detail rather than a measured analyte. It has no direct relevance to liver function, PBC, or cirrhosis monitoring and should not be tracked as part of liver disease surveillance; the report's own reference range is nan-nan (i.e., no meaningful normal range applies), so no numeric thresholds should be shown to the patient.

This is a qualitative urinalysis parameter (normally reported as "clear/transparent") and is not a liver-specific marker — it's typically used to screen for urinary tract infection, crystalluria, or kidney issues rather than to monitor PBC or cirrhosis. Cloudiness can occasionally be seen with bilirubinuria in cholestatic liver disease, but it is a nonspecific, low-value sign for liver monitoring; ALP, GGT, bilirubin, and albumin remain the relevant markers for PBC/cirrhosis tracking.

This is a urinalysis marker reflecting kidney concentrating ability and hydration status, not a liver-specific test. It is not typically used to monitor PBC or liver cirrhosis progression directly, though in advanced cirrhosis with ascites or hepatorenal syndrome it may be tracked as part of general renal/fluid status assessment rather than liver function itself.

This is a urinalysis marker (protein in urine, i.e., proteinuria), not a liver-specific test -- it's normally used to screen for kidney disease/damage rather than liver function. In PBC/cirrhosis patients it can become relevant only indirectly, e.g., if hepatorenal syndrome, advanced ascites, or coexisting kidney disease develops, but it does not directly track liver fibrosis or cholestasis like ALP, GGT, or bilirubin do.

This is a qualitative urinalysis parameter (normal is "straw/light yellow"), not a specific liver marker; it's typically assessed for hydration status, kidney/urinary tract conditions, or hemolysis. That said, in liver disease dark yellow-brown or "tea-colored" urine can appear due to elevated conjugated bilirubin, so it may be a nonspecific supportive sign of cholestasis in PBC, but should never be relied on alone to monitor liver status.

This is a urinalysis parameter (urine acidity/alkalinity) and is not a liver-specific marker — it is not used to monitor PBC or cirrhosis progression. Urine pH is typically tracked for kidney stone risk, urinary tract infections, diet, or metabolic/acid-base disturbances rather than liver function.

This is a urine sediment marker (squamous epithelial cell count from urinalysis), not a liver-specific test — it mainly reflects genitourinary tract lining cells and is used to assess urine sample quality/contamination or urinary tract irritation, not liver or bile duct function. For PBC/cirrhosis monitoring, it has no direct diagnostic relevance and should not be used to track disease progression; it may still be checked incidentally as part of routine urinalysis panels.

This is a urine sediment marker reflecting cells shed from the bladder/urinary tract lining (renal pelvis, ureters, bladder), not a liver-specific test — it's typically used to screen for urinary tract irritation, infection, or inflammation rather than to monitor PBC or cirrhosis. It has no direct role in tracking liver disease progression; elevated values in a cirrhosis patient would usually prompt evaluation for a urinary issue rather than a hepatic one.

This is a urine sediment marker reflecting renal tubular epithelial cell shedding, used to assess kidney (not liver) health — e.g., detecting tubular damage, nephritis, or other renal pathology. It is not a marker of PBC or liver cirrhosis, though clinicians may still monitor renal function in cirrhotic patients (e.g., for hepatorenal syndrome) using other tests like creatinine and urea rather than this one directly.

This is a urine sediment marker (white blood cell count in urine, typically from automated urinalysis) and is not a liver-specific test — it's used to screen for urinary tract infection or inflammation, not for monitoring PBC or cirrhosis. In a PBC/cirrhosis patient it may still be tracked incidentally as part of routine urinalysis, but changes here should not be interpreted as reflecting liver disease progression; ascitic fluid or blood leukocyte counts (e.g., WBC) are more relevant if infection (like SBP) is a concern.

This is a urine sediment finding (clumped leukocytes seen on urinalysis), not a liver-specific marker — it is used to screen for urinary tract infection or inflammation, not for monitoring PBC or cirrhosis. It should be tracked alongside other urine parameters (e.g. WBC_URINE, EPITHELIAL cells) rather than as a liver marker; however, cirrhotic patients are at higher risk of UTIs/spontaneous infections generally, so an elevated value is still worth flagging to the treating physician.

This is a urine sediment marker (unchanged/non-hemolyzed red blood cells per microliter), not a liver-specific test - it's used to screen for hematuria and its urinary tract source (e.g., glomerular vs. lower urinary tract bleeding). It has no direct role in monitoring PBC or liver cirrhosis, though cirrhotic patients with coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia can occasionally show incidental hematuria, which this marker would help detect.

This is a urine sediment marker (dysmorphic/altered red blood cells, typically of glomerular origin) and is not a liver-specific test — it is used to help distinguish glomerular vs non-glomerular sources of hematuria in kidney/urinary tract evaluation. It has no direct role in monitoring PBC or liver cirrhosis, though clinicians may check it incidentally if renal function or urinalysis abnormalities arise as a complication (e.g., hepatorenal concerns) in advanced liver disease.

This is a urine sediment marker reflecting kidney tubule status, not a liver-specific test — it is not part of routine PBC/cirrhosis monitoring. It's usually tracked for general kidney function/dehydration screening or as part of a routine urinalysis; hyaline casts can appear transiently with dehydration, fever, or exercise and are often not clinically significant in small amounts. In cirrhosis patients it may be watched incidentally if hepatorenal syndrome or other kidney complications are a concern, but it does not indicate liver damage itself.

This is a urine sediment marker reflecting kidney tubular pathology (chronic/advanced renal disease, nephrotic syndrome), not a liver-specific test. It is not used to monitor PBC or liver cirrhosis directly, though in advanced cirrhosis with hepatorenal syndrome or concurrent kidney disease it could appear as part of general renal function assessment.

This is a urine sediment parameter (from automated urinalysis) and is not a liver-specific marker; it is not used to monitor PBC or cirrhosis. Elevated mucus in urine is typically nonspecific or related to genitourinary tract conditions (e.g., contamination from genital secretions, urinary tract irritation/infection) rather than liver disease.

This is not a liver-specific marker — it's a routine urine sediment/microscopy finding reflecting crystallized salts (e.g., urates, oxalates, phosphates) in urine, typically used to assess hydration, diet, or risk of kidney stones/urinary tract issues. It is not part of standard PBC or liver cirrhosis monitoring, though advanced cirrhosis patients occasionally have urinalysis done as part of general health or kidney function screening (e.g., for hepatorenal concerns), in which case this value would just be one incidental part of that broader panel.

This is a urine sediment finding, not a liver-specific marker — it reflects urinary crystal formation (related to diet, hydration, kidney stone risk, or oxalate metabolism) rather than liver or bile duct function. It is not part of standard PBC/cirrhosis monitoring, though cirrhotic patients with poor fluid intake or diuretic use may occasionally show incidental crystalluria; it should be interpreted in the context of renal/urinary health, not liver disease progression.

This is a urine sediment finding (microscopic crystal count), not a liver-specific marker — it reflects urine pH, hydration, and purine/uric acid metabolism, and is typically used to screen for risk of uric acid stones or gout-related crystalluria rather than to monitor PBC or liver cirrhosis. It may be mildly elevated in some cirrhotic patients due to altered uric acid handling or concentrated urine, but it is not a standard tool for tracking liver disease progression.

This is a urine sediment finding (a type of crystal, often "struvite" - magnesium ammonium phosphate) and is not a liver-specific marker; it is not used to monitor PBC or cirrhosis. It's typically evaluated in urinalysis to assess urine chemistry, alkaline pH, and risk of struvite kidney stones or urinary tract infection with urease-producing bacteria.

This is a urinalysis sediment finding (crystal count on automated urine microscopy), not a liver-specific marker. It's typically tracked for kidney stone risk, urine pH/concentration issues, and gout/purine metabolism rather than for monitoring PBC or liver cirrhosis; in a cirrhosis patient it might reflect dehydration or diuretic use but doesn't directly indicate liver disease activity.

This is a urine sediment finding (crystal count), not a liver-specific marker — ammonium urate crystals typically relate to urine pH, hydration, and are often seen in infants, stool/urine stasis, or chronic diarrhea/laxative use rather than liver disease. In PBC/cirrhosis it is not a standard marker to track; it's usually monitored as part of routine urinalysis for urinary tract/metabolic issues, not for liver function or fibrosis progression.

This is a urine sediment microscopy parameter (amorphous urates/phosphates seen on automated urinalysis), not a liver-specific marker — it reflects urine crystal/salt precipitation influenced by pH, hydration and diet, and is not used to monitor PBC or cirrhosis progression. Liver status in PBC is better tracked via ALP, GGT, bilirubin, albumin and AMA-M2.

This is a urine sediment finding (crystallized urate salts, often from concentrated/acidic urine or high purine intake) and is not a liver-specific marker. It's typically tracked for urinary tract/kidney stone risk and hydration status rather than for monitoring PBC or liver cirrhosis progression.

This is a urine sediment microscopy finding (crystallized phosphate salts, often from alkaline or concentrated urine, diet, or standing sample) and is not a liver-specific marker. It is not used to monitor PBC or cirrhosis progression; it's typically noted incidentally on urinalysis and is usually benign unless persistently elevated with other urinary abnormalities suggesting infection or metabolic/stone risk.

This is not a liver-specific marker — it's a urinalysis parameter reflecting bacterial presence in urine, typically used to screen for urinary tract infection. It has no direct relevance to PBC or cirrhosis monitoring, though clinicians may check it incidentally as part of routine labs, especially in patients with ascites who need to be monitored for infection risk in general.

This is not a liver-specific marker at all — it is a urine sediment finding (presence of spermatozoa in urine, e.g. after intercourse or retrograde ejaculation) that has no relevance to PBC or liver cirrhosis monitoring. It is typically noted incidentally during a general urinalysis rather than tracked for any disease process, and can be safely ignored in the context of liver disease follow-up.

This is a urine sediment microscopy finding (yeast cells, typically Candida) and is not a liver-specific marker at all - it reflects urinary tract or genital contamination/infection risk, not liver function or fibrosis. It is usually tracked for urinary tract or fungal infection screening; in cirrhosis patients it may be watched somewhat more closely only because immune compromise or diabetes (sometimes comorbid) can predispose to candiduria, but it does not indicate cholangitis or cirrhosis progression itself.

This is a urine sediment microscopy finding indicating fungal (yeast, e.g. Candida) presence with pseudohyphae, not a liver-specific marker. It is generally used to detect urinary tract or genital fungal contamination/infection rather than to monitor PBC or cirrhosis progression, though immunosuppressed or diabetic cirrhosis patients may be more prone to such infections.

markers.marker_name_en: Budding yeast cells (repeat test), urine sediment
markers.cirrhosis_note: This is a urine microscopy finding (presence of budding yeast, e.g. Candida, in urine sediment) and is not a liver-specific marker. It is generally not used to monitor PBC or cirrhosis progression; it's typically checked to screen for urinary tract or genital yeast infection, or contamination of the sample, and can be more common in diabetic or immunocompromised patients rather than reflecting liver disease activity.
